Are there infinitely many positive integers not of the form $n-\phi(n)$?
#418: [Er74b,p.201][ErGr80,p.103]
number theory
Asked by Erdős and Sierpiński. Numbers not of the form we call non-cototients. It follows from the Goldbach conjecture that every odd number can be written as $n-\phi(n)$. What happens for even numbers?
Browkin and Schinzel [BrSc95] provided an affirmative answer to this question, proving that any integer of the shape $2^{k}\cdot 509203$ for $k\geq 1$ is a non-cototient. It is open whether the set of non-cototients has positive density.
Erdős [Er73b] has shown that a positive density set of natural numbers cannot be written as $\sigma(n)-n$ (numbers not of this form are called nonaliquot, or sometimes untouchable). Banks and Luca [BaLu05] have proved that the set of nonaliquots has lower density $\geq 1/48$. This bound was improved to $0.06$ by Chen and Zhao [ChZh11]. Pollack and Pomerance [PoPo16] give a heuristic that predicts the density exactly (with a value of $\approx 0.17$).
This is discussed in problem B36 of Guy's collection [Gu04]. 
Additional thanks to: Stefan Steinerberger and Wouter van Doorn

 We say that a positive integer is a noncototient if it cannot be written as $n - \phi(n)$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$. OEIS sequence A263958 provides a sequence of known integers $m$ such that $m2^k$ is a noncototient for all $k \ge 1$. The smallest of these $m$ is $509203$, which -as mentioned- was obtained by Browkin and Schinzel in [BrSc95]. See this paper by Flammenkamp and Luca for more information on some of the other values of $m$ for which this is true.
Even though the question whether the set of noncototients has positive lower density has indeed not been settled as far as I know, Banks and Luca do prove in this paper that for almost all primes $p$, the integer $2p$ is a noncototient. So we have a lower bound of $\frac{(\frac{1}{2}+o(1))x}{\log x}$ for the number of noncototients below $x$. Incidentally, in this same paper they furthermore show that the lower density for elements not of the form $\sigma(n) - n$ (which [Er73b] proved the positivity of) is at least $\frac{1}{48}$.

 I don't think this is quite right. You state that these integers are called noncotients or nonaliquots, but they are not the same. A noncotient is any positive integer that cannot be written as $n - \phi(n)$. A nonaliquot is any positive integer that cannot be written as $\sigma(n) - n$. 
Erdős proved that the set of nonaliquots has positive density. Banks and Luca did then indeed show that this lower density is at least $\frac{1}{48}$ (improving a lower bound of $0.0324$ by te Riele), with Chen and Zhao improving it further to some constant larger than $0.06$. Pollack and Pomerance (see Conjecture 1.4) put forth a conjecture for the exact density of nonaliquots.
However, corresponding density results for the set of noncotients are, as far as I can tell, not known.
